subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: On a velocity–time graph, what does the area under the line represent?
questions.explain: The area under a velocity–time graph equals velocity × time, which gives the distance travelled. The gradient gives the acceleration.

questions.q: Which of these is the correct SI base unit of mass?
questions.explain: The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram (kg). The gram is a smaller unit, the newton is the unit of force, and the pound is not an SI unit.

questions.q: Why does light bend (refract) when it passes from air into glass?
options: It speeds up in the glass
Its speed changes, which changes its direction (unless it hits the boundary along the normal)
questions.explain: Refraction happens because the wave changes speed when it enters a different medium. Light slows down in glass; if it meets the boundary at an angle, this change of speed bends it toward the normal.

questions.q: How do all electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum?
options: At different speeds depending on frequency
All at the same speed (the speed of light)
They cannot travel through a vacuum
Only visible light can travel through a vacuum
questions.explain: All EM waves are transverse and travel at the same speed (about 3 × 10⁸ m/s) through a vacuum. They differ in frequency and wavelength, not speed in a vacuum.

questions.q: For a stable orbit, if a satellite moves to a larger orbital radius, what must happen to its speed?
options: It cannot stay in orbit at a larger radius
Its speed stays exactly the same
questions.explain: For a stable orbit at a given radius there is only one possible speed. A larger orbital radius requires a slower orbital speed; a smaller radius requires a faster speed.

questions.q: Why does atmospheric pressure decrease as you go higher up a mountain?
options: There is less air (a shorter column of air) above you pressing down
questions.explain: Atmospheric pressure is caused by the weight of the air above. Higher up, there is less air above you and it is less dense, so the pressure is lower.

questions.q: As you go deeper into a liquid, what happens to the pressure?
questions.explain: Pressure in a fluid increases with depth because there is a greater weight of fluid above pushing down (p = hρg).

questions.q: An object floats on water. How does the upthrust compare with the object's weight?
options: Upthrust is less than the weight
Upthrust is greater than the weight
questions.explain: A floating object is in equilibrium, so the upthrust (upward) exactly balances the weight (downward). If upthrust were less, it would sink; if more, it would rise.

questions.q: When light passes from glass into air (along a line not on the normal), it bends:
options: Towards the normal because it slows down
It does not bend at all
Away from the normal because it speeds up
questions.explain: Light speeds up when it enters a less dense medium (glass to air), so it refracts away from the normal.

questions.q: What is the difference between elastic and inelastic deformation?
options: Elastic deformation is permanent; inelastic returns to shape
Elastic deformation returns to the original shape when the force is removed; inelastic does not
questions.explain: In elastic deformation the object returns to its original shape once the force is removed. In inelastic (plastic) deformation it does not fully return — it is permanently changed.

questions.q: As light passes from air into a glass block along a path at an angle to the normal, it bends:
options: Away from the normal because it speeds up
Straight back the way it came
It does not bend at all
Toward the normal because it slows down
questions.explain: Glass is more optically dense than air, so light slows down on entering. This makes the ray bend toward the normal. Going the other way (glass to air) it speeds up and bends away from the normal.

questions.q: An object is partly submerged in water. What causes the upthrust on it?
options: The water pressure is greater on the bottom than on the top of the object
The object is lighter than air
questions.explain: Pressure in a fluid increases with depth, so the upward pressure on the bottom of the object is greater than the downward pressure on its top. This difference produces a net upward force called upthrust.

questions.q: A spacecraft moves through deep space with its engines off and no resultant force acting. According to Newton's first law, what happens?
options: It continues at constant velocity in a straight line
It gradually slows down and stops
questions.explain: Newton's first law: with no resultant force, an object continues at constant velocity (here in a straight line at steady speed). This tendency to keep its motion is called inertia.

questions.q: What does it mean if a spring is stretched beyond its limit of proportionality?
options: The extension is no longer directly proportional to the force
No more force is needed to stretch it
questions.explain: Beyond the limit of proportionality the force–extension graph is no longer a straight line, so extension is no longer directly proportional to force (and deformation may become inelastic).

questions.q: An object floats when the upthrust acting on it is:
questions.explain: When floating, the upthrust (upward force from the fluid) balances the object's weight, so the resultant force is zero. If weight exceeds the maximum upthrust, the object sinks.

questions.q: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Which factor increases the thinking distance?
questions.explain: Thinking distance depends on reaction time, increased by tiredness, alcohol or distractions. Worn brakes, ice and bald tyres increase the braking distance instead.

questions.q: When ice melts to form water, what happens to the total mass?
questions.explain: Melting is a physical change: no particles are created or destroyed, so mass is conserved. The water has the same mass as the ice it came from.

questions.q: In what direction do magnetic field lines around a bar magnet point?
options: From south pole to north pole outside the magnet
From north pole to south pole outside the magnet
questions.explain: By convention, magnetic field lines travel from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet. The direction is the direction of the force on a north pole.

questions.q: On a force–extension graph for a spring obeying Hooke's law, the line is:
options: A straight line through the origin
questions.explain: While a spring obeys Hooke's law, force is directly proportional to extension, so the force–extension graph is a straight line through the origin. The gradient equals the spring constant k.

questions.q: Which statement about force is correct?
options: Force has direction but no size
Force is a scalar with magnitude only
Force is a vector with both magnitude and direction
questions.explain: Force is a vector quantity: it has both a magnitude and a direction, and is measured in newtons (N). This is why forces are drawn as arrows.

questions.q: An object moves at a steady speed in a circular orbit. Why is it still accelerating?
options: Its direction (and therefore velocity) is constantly changing
It is moving in a straight line
questions.explain: Velocity is a vector. Even at constant speed, the direction is continuously changing in a circular orbit, so the velocity changes — this change in velocity is the (centripetal) acceleration.

questions.q: What happens to atmospheric pressure as you climb to a higher altitude?
questions.explain: As altitude increases there is less air above you, so the weight pressing down is smaller and atmospheric pressure decreases.
